label: Poverty Point earthworks
note: Documented site: the Poverty Point earthworks and plaza near Epps, built about 1700 to 1100 BCE and described by UNESCO as used for residential and ceremonial purposes; no instruments are known from it.
sources: 64 Parishes, Poverty Point <https://64parishes.org/entry/poverty-point> | UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Monumental Earthworks of Poverty Point <https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1435>

label: Marksville and Troyville mound centers
note: Documented sites: the Marksville and Greenhouse sites (Avoyelles), the Crooks mound (LaSalle), where burials held pebble clusters that were probably rattles, and Troyville (Catahoula), where archaeologists infer feasting and public ceremony.
sources: 64 Parishes, Marksville Culture <https://64parishes.org/entry/marksville-culture> | 64 Parishes, Troyville Culture <https://64parishes.org/entry/troyville-culture>

label: Early Caddo ceremonial centers
note: Documented sites: the Mounds Plantation and Belcher mounds (Caddo Parish) and the Gahagan site (Red River Parish), source of an effigy pipe showing a frog holding a ceremonial rattle.
sources: 64 Parishes, Caddo Culture <https://64parishes.org/entry/caddo-culture> | Neuman and Hawkins, Louisiana Prehistory, Louisiana Archaeological Survey and Antiquities Commission <https://www.mirrorservice.org/sites/ftp.ibiblio.org/pub/docs/books/gutenberg/6/2/1/8/62189/62189-h/62189-h.htm>

label: Caddo homeland on the Red River
parishes: Caddo; Red River; De Soto; Natchitoches
note: Historic homeland of the Caddo, whose Turkey Dance songs recall the creation of Caddo Lake; it ends with the 1835 cession, after which the Caddo Nation's home became Oklahoma.
sources: 64 Parishes, Caddo Nation <https://64parishes.org/entry/caddo-nation> | 64 Parishes, Caddo Culture <https://64parishes.org/entry/caddo-culture>

label: Chitimacha homeland
parishes: St. Mary; St. Martin; Iberia; Iberville; Assumption
note: Historic homeland as the Chitimacha describe it, centered on the Atchafalaya Basin, Bayou Teche and upper Bayou Lafourche; a conservative subset of a territory the tribe says reached the Gulf and the New Orleans area.
sources: Chitimacha Tribe of Louisiana, Tribal History <https://www.chitimacha.gov/history-culture/tribal-history> | Louisiana Folklife Program, Louisiana Indians in the 21st Century <https://www.louisianafolklife.org/lt/articles_essays/nativeams.html>

label: Tribal homelands today
parishes: Avoyelles; Allen; St. Mary; LaSalle; Terrebonne; Lafourche
note: Present homelands: Tunica-Biloxi at Marksville, Coushatta near Elton, Chitimacha at Charenton, Jena Band of Choctaw at Jena, and the United Houma Nation on the Terrebonne and Lafourche bayous, all in place by the 1880s.
sources: Tunica-Biloxi Tribe of Louisiana, History <https://www.tunicabiloxi.org/history/> | 64 Parishes, Coushatta Tribe of Louisiana <https://64parishes.org/entry/coushatta-tribe-of-louisiana> | Chitimacha Tribe of Louisiana, Tribal History <https://www.chitimacha.gov/history-culture/tribal-history> | 64 Parishes, Jena Band of the Choctaw Tribe <https://64parishes.org/entry/jena-band-of-the-choctaw-tribe> | 64 Parishes, Houma Nation <https://64parishes.org/entry/houma-nation> | Louisiana Folklife Program, H.F. Gregory, A Promise From the Sun <https://www.louisianafolklife.org/lt/virtual_books/Guide_to_state/gregory.html>

label: Colonial New Orleans
note: Every dated colonial musical event in the sources, from the 1725 parish musician to the 1796 opera, took place in New Orleans.
sources: 64 Parishes, Classical Music in Louisiana <https://64parishes.org/entry/classical-music-in-louisiana> | 64 Parishes, Opera and Ballet <https://64parishes.org/entry/opera-and-ballet>

label: Congo Square and New Orleans
note: Sunday gatherings of enslaved Africans are documented in and around New Orleans and, from 1817, at Congo Square itself.
sources: 64 Parishes, Congo Square <https://64parishes.org/entry/congo-square> | 64 Parishes, Congo Square: La Place Publique <https://64parishes.org/congo-square-la-place-publique> | New Orleans Historical, Congo Square: Mythology and Music <https://neworleanshistorical.org/items/show/745>

label: Creole prairie heartland
parishes: St. Landry; Evangeline; St. Martin; Jefferson Davis
note: Sources place la-la house dances and their players in the prairie country between Eunice and Basile, at Duralde and around Lawtell; the Lomaxes recorded jure singers near Jennings and Lake Arthur in 1934; St. Martinville is named as a Creole community and zydeco town. The 1900 start is a round number for the early twentieth century.
sources: 64 Parishes, Amede Ardoin <https://64parishes.org/entry/amede-ardoin> | 64 Parishes, Zydeco <https://64parishes.org/entry/zydeco-music> | Louisiana Folklife Program, Nicholas Spitzer, The Creole State <https://www.louisianafolklife.org/lt/articles_essays/creole_art_creole_state.html> | Louisiana Folklife Program, Barry Jean Ancelet, Lomax in Louisiana: Trials and Triumph <https://www.louisianafolklife.org/LT/Articles_Essays/LFMlomax.html> | 64 Parishes, Bois Sec Ardoin <https://64parishes.org/entry/bois-sec-ardoin>

label: Acadian settlements
parishes: St. Martin; Iberia; St. Landry; St. James; Ascension; Iberville; Assumption; Lafourche
note: Parishes where Brasseaux documents Acadian settlement between 1765 and 1785: the Attakapas district, including Fausse Pointe, and the neighboring Opelousas district; the Acadian Coast; St. Gabriel; and, from 1785, Bayou Lafourche between Labadieville and Raceland.
sources: Acadian Memorial, Carl Brasseaux, Acadian Immigration Into South Louisiana 1764-1785 <https://acadianmemorial.org/acadian-immigration-into-south-louisiana-1764-1785/> | 64 Parishes, Cajuns <https://64parishes.org/entry/cajuns>

label: Cajun prairie heartland
parishes: Lafayette; Acadia; St. Landry; Evangeline; Jefferson Davis; Calcasieu; St. Martin; Vermilion; Iberia
note: Sandmel places Cajun music in Lafayette, Lake Charles, Eunice, Opelousas and the prairies between them; Rayne, Ville Platte and Breaux Bridge are named by Ancelet and 64 Parishes; the Lomaxes recorded Cajun singers at Kaplan, Erath and New Iberia in 1934, and Nathan Abshire grew up near Gueydan. The 1900 start is a round number for Ancelet's turn of the twentieth century.
sources: Louisiana Folklife Program, Ben Sandmel, The Treasured Traditions of Louisiana Music <https://www.louisianafolklife.org/LT/Articles_Essays/treas_trad_la_music.html> | 64 Parishes, Cajun Music <https://64parishes.org/entry/cajun-music> | Louisiana Folklife Program, Barry Ancelet, Cajun and Zydeco Music Traditions <https://www.louisianafolklife.org/lt/articles_essays/cajunzydeco.html> | Louisiana Folklife Program, Barry Jean Ancelet, Lomax in Louisiana: Trials and Triumph <https://www.louisianafolklife.org/LT/Articles_Essays/LFMlomax.html> | 64 Parishes, Nathan Abshire <https://64parishes.org/entry/nathan-abshire>

label: Zydeco heartland
parishes: St. Landry; Lafayette; St. Martin; Calcasieu
note: Parishes of the towns the 64 Parishes entry names as zydeco ground: Opelousas and Lawtell, Lafayette, St. Martinville and Lake Charles.
sources: 64 Parishes, Zydeco <https://64parishes.org/entry/zydeco-music> | Louisiana Folklife Program, Ben Sandmel, The Treasured Traditions of Louisiana Music <https://www.louisianafolklife.org/LT/Articles_Essays/treas_trad_la_music.html>

label: New Orleans, birthplace of jazz
note: All sources locate the emergence of jazz in New Orleans, beginning with Buddy Bolden's band in 1895.
sources: National Park Service, Jazz Origins in New Orleans <https://www.nps.gov/jazz/learn/historyculture/history_early.htm> | National Park Service, A New Orleans Jazz History 1895-1927 <https://www.nps.gov/jazz/learn/historyculture/jazz_history.htm> | 64 Parishes, Traditional New Orleans Jazz <https://64parishes.org/entry/traditional-new-orleans-jazz>

label: Lake and river parish dance halls
parishes: St. Tammany; St. John the Baptist
note: Early jazz is documented at Mandeville's Dew Drop hall, built in 1895 and active until about 1940, and in Kid Ory's Woodland Band near LaPlace, photographed in 1905.
sources: 64 Parishes, Dew Drop Social and Benevolent Jazz Hall <https://64parishes.org/?p=60743> | 64 Parishes, The Woodland Band (photograph, Hogan Jazz Archive) <https://64parishes.org/entry-image/the-woodland-band>

label: New Orleans brass band and second line
note: Brass bands, jazz funerals and social aid and pleasure club parades are documented as New Orleans street traditions.
sources: 64 Parishes, Brass Bands of New Orleans <https://64parishes.org/entry/brass-bands-of-new-orleans> | 64 Parishes, Jazz Funerals and Second Line Parades <https://64parishes.org/entry/jazz-funerals-and-second-line-parades> | National Park Service, Jazz Origins in New Orleans <https://www.nps.gov/jazz/learn/historyculture/history_early.htm>

label: Mardi Gras Indian New Orleans
note: Mardi Gras Indian gangs belong to New Orleans neighborhoods, Uptown, Downtown and the West Bank.
sources: 64 Parishes, Mardi Gras Indians <https://64parishes.org/entry/mardi-gras-indians> | 64 Parishes, Allison Tootie Montana <https://64parishes.org/entry/allison-tootie-montana>

label: Shreveport blues
note: Shreveport is named as a center of guitar blues through the first half of the twentieth century, from Lead Belly's Fannin Street to postwar KWKH and Jewel sessions.
sources: 64 Parishes, Blues Music <https://64parishes.org/entry/blues-music> | Louisiana Folklife Program, Ben Sandmel, The Blues in Louisiana <https://www.louisianafolklife.org/LT/Articles_Essays/blues.html>

label: Delta and northeast blues
note: Folklife fieldwork documents country blues players at Waterproof, Tallulah and Rayville, and sources name Ferriday and Monroe as blues towns; the start year is approximate.
sources: Louisiana Folklife Program, Ben Sandmel, The Blues in Louisiana <https://www.louisianafolklife.org/LT/Articles_Essays/blues.html> | Louisiana Folklife Program, Ben Sandmel, The Treasured Traditions of Louisiana Music <https://www.louisianafolklife.org/LT/Articles_Essays/treas_trad_la_music.html> | 64 Parishes, Blues Music <https://64parishes.org/entry/blues-music>

label: Baton Rouge swamp blues country
parishes: East Baton Rouge; West Baton Rouge; Pointe Coupee; East Feliciana; West Feliciana
note: Jackson traces Baton Rouge blues to 1930s farming communities at Zachary, Clinton, Slaughter and St. Francisville and to players from West Baton Rouge and Pointe Coupee; the records were made in Crowley, outside the region.
sources: Louisiana Folklife Program, Joyce Jackson, Blues and Blacks in the Red Stick <https://www.louisianafolklife.org/LT/Articles_Essays/brblues1.html> | 64 Parishes, Blues Music <https://64parishes.org/entry/blues-music>

label: Delta spirituals and Easter Rock
note: Parishes where Roach documents the Easter Rock, a spiritual-singing ritual remembered as older than the Civil War: Winnsboro in Franklin, Clayton and Ferriday in Concordia, and as far north as Lake Providence in East Carroll; the start year is approximate.
sources: Louisiana Folklife Program, Susan Roach, Continuity and Creativity in the Louisiana Delta Easter Rock <https://www.louisianafolklife.org/LT/Articles_Essays/easterrock.html> | Louisiana Folklife Program, Gospel Music in Louisiana <https://www.louisianafolklife.org/lt/articles_essays/gospel_music_in_la.html>

label: North Louisiana gospel belt
parishes: Caddo; Webster; Ouachita; Rapides; West Carroll
note: Parishes of the north and central Louisiana towns the sources name for quartets, family groups and singing conventions: Shreveport, Cotton Valley, Monroe, Pineville and Oak Grove. The start year is approximate; the earliest dated Louisiana events in the sources are from the 1930s.
sources: 64 Parishes, White Gospel Music <https://64parishes.org/entry/white-gospel-music> | 64 Parishes, Black Gospel Music <https://64parishes.org/entry/black-gospel-music> | Louisiana Folklife Program, Gospel Music in Louisiana <https://www.louisianafolklife.org/lt/articles_essays/gospel_music_in_la.html>

label: New Orleans and Baton Rouge gospel
note: Quartet singing in New Orleans is dated to the 1910s, and the sources name Mahalia Jackson and the Zion Harmonizers there and the Zion Travelers and Harvey Herron in Baton Rouge.
sources: 64 Parishes, Black Gospel Music <https://64parishes.org/entry/black-gospel-music> | Louisiana Folklife Program, Gospel Music in Louisiana <https://www.louisianafolklife.org/lt/articles_essays/gospel_music_in_la.html>

label: North Louisiana country and Hayride territory
note: Shreveport's KWKH and Louisiana Hayride anchor the region; Dubach fiddler Hiter Colvin, the Cox Family of Cotton Valley and Monroe are named in the sources.
sources: 64 Parishes, Country Music <https://64parishes.org/entry/country-music> | 64 Parishes, Louisiana Hayride <https://64parishes.org/entry/louisiana-hayride> | Louisiana Folklife Program, Ben Sandmel, The Treasured Traditions of Louisiana Music <https://www.louisianafolklife.org/LT/Articles_Essays/treas_trad_la_music.html>

label: New Orleans rhythm and blues
note: The style is defined by records made at J&M and later New Orleans studios.
sources: 64 Parishes, Rhythm and Blues Music <https://64parishes.org/entry/rhythm-and-blues-music> | Louisiana Folklife Program, Ben Sandmel, The Treasured Traditions of Louisiana Music <https://www.louisianafolklife.org/LT/Articles_Essays/treas_trad_la_music.html>

label: Swamp pop Acadiana
parishes: St. Landry; Lafayette; Calcasieu; Evangeline; Iberia; Acadia
note: Parishes of the Acadiana towns Shane Bernard names: Opelousas, Lafayette, Lake Charles and Vinton, Ville Platte, New Iberia and Crowley.
sources: 64 Parishes, Swamp Pop <https://64parishes.org/entry/swamp-pop-music>

label: Swamp pop river and bayou parishes
note: Joe Barry of Cut Off in Lafourche Parish had a national swamp pop hit in 1961, and Bernard names Ascension, Assumption, Terrebonne and Lafourche as parishes between Baton Rouge and New Orleans where the music's popularity has grown among later generations. The start year is approximate, and most of this eastward spread is later than the 1960s.
sources: 64 Parishes, Swamp Pop <https://64parishes.org/entry/swamp-pop-music> | WWNO and NPR, The Unsung Pioneer of Louisiana Swamp Pop <https://www.wwno.org/post/unsung-pioneer-louisiana-swamp-pop>

label: New Orleans funk
note: The Meters and the studio scene around Allen Toussaint were based in New Orleans.
sources: 64 Parishes, The Meters <https://64parishes.org/entry/the-meters/> | 64 Parishes, Rhythm and Blues Music <https://64parishes.org/entry/rhythm-and-blues-music>

label: New Orleans bounce
note: Bounce began in the Hollygrove neighborhood and the sources describe it as a New Orleans music.
sources: 64 Parishes, Bounce <https://64parishes.org/entry/bounce> | 64 Parishes, Rap, Hip-Hop, and Bounce Music <https://64parishes.org/entry/rap-hip-hop-and-bounce-music>

label: New Orleans hip-hop
note: Early crews and the Cash Money and No Limit labels were based in New Orleans.
sources: 64 Parishes, Rap, Hip-Hop, and Bounce Music <https://64parishes.org/entry/rap-hip-hop-and-bounce-music>

label: Baton Rouge hip-hop
note: Baton Rouge's scene dates to the late 1990s with Young Bleed and C-Loc, followed by Boosie's 2000 debut; the start year is approximate.
sources: XXL, 12 Baton Rouge Rappers You Should Know <https://www.xxlmag.com/baton-rouge-rappers-you-should-know/> | 64 Parishes, Rap, Hip-Hop, and Bounce Music <https://64parishes.org/entry/rap-hip-hop-and-bounce-music>

label: Creole songs of Good Hope plantation
note: Documented source: the seven Louisiana Creole songs printed in Slave Songs of the United States (1867), a calinda among them, were written down from a woman who heard them sung before the Civil War on Good Hope plantation in St. Charles Parish. The songs are older than their publication, and Creole singing was not confined to this parish.
sources: Allen, Ware and Garrison, Slave Songs of the United States (1867), Documenting the American South <https://docsouth.unc.edu/church/allen/allen.html>

label: New Orleans opera houses and concert life
note: The dated events used for this genre all took place in New Orleans, from the 1796 Sylvain at the Théâtre St. Pierre through the Théâtre d'Orléans and French Opera House to the sacred concerts, church choirs and music stores of the antebellum American sector, so the region is limited to Orleans Parish. 64 Parishes also records later companies elsewhere in the state, such as Opéra Louisiane in Baton Rouge (2006); those are not mapped here.
sources: 64 Parishes, Opera and Ballet <https://64parishes.org/entry/opera-and-ballet> | 64 Parishes, Classical Music in Louisiana by Alfred E. Lemmon <https://64parishes.org/entry/classical-music-in-louisiana> | Warren Keith Kimball, Northern Music Culture in Antebellum New Orleans (PhD diss., Louisiana State University, 2017), abstract (p. iv) and chs. 1-4 (pp. 1-114) <https://repository.lsu.edu/gradschool_dissertations/4119>

label: Baton Rouge university bands (LSU and Southern)
note: LSU's cadet band was organized in Baton Rouge in 1893, and Southern University's marching band, later the Human Jukebox, was established there in 1947.
sources: LSU Department of Bands, Mission and History <https://lsu.edu/cmda/bands/mission-and-history/index.php> | WAFB, A brief history of the Southern University Human Jukebox Marching Band <https://www.wafb.com/story/38060598/a-brief-history-of-the-southern-university-human-jukebox-marching-band/>

label: Grambling's World Famed Tiger Marching Band
note: Grambling's band began in 1926 with seventeen instruments obtained by Ralph Waldo Emerson Jones, and Conrad Hutchinson Jr. directed it from 1952.
sources: Grambling State University, GSU Tiger Marching Band history <https://www.gram.edu/academics/majors/arts-and-sciences/music/band/history.php> | Bayou Classic, Since 1974 <https://mybayouclassic.com/since-1974/>

label: New Orleans school bands and Carnival parades
note: Edwin Hampton started the St. Augustine High School band, later the Marching 100, in 1952 and Donald Richardson started Bell Junior High's Marching Crusaders in 1963; the city's school bands march in Carnival parades, and it has hosted the Bayou Classic since 1974.
sources: OffBeat, Jeff Hannusch, Mardi Gras with the St. Augustine High School Marching 100 (1999) <https://offbeat.com/articles/mardi-gras-with-the-st-augustine-high-school-marching-100> | A Closer Walk (Ponderosa Stomp Foundation and WWOZ), Bell Junior High School <https://acloserwalknola.com/places/bell-junior-high-school/> | WWNO New Orleans Public Radio via HPPR, With the return of Mardi Gras marching bands (2022) <https://www.hppr.org/2022-03-01/with-the-return-of-mardi-gras-marching-bands-new-orleans-streets-are-full-of-magic> | Bayou Classic, Since 1974 <https://mybayouclassic.com/since-1974/>
